1:
After the seven days' silence Job breaks it, and the witnesses gather first around the fact that the poetry of the book begins precisely here. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the seam plainly: with this chapter “the poetic part of the book begins,” for nothing in the preceding chapters has either the form or the spirit of Hebrew verse; the narrative frame is prose, and only now does Job's speech rise into the impassioned hemistichs of a lament. Clarke hears in the execration something “awfully solemn, tremendously deep, and strikingly sublime,” yet refuses to excuse all that a suffering man says in the bitterness of his soul: Job, in heaviness through manifold temptation and perhaps with the light of God withdrawn from his mind, regrets that ever he was born, and in a high strain of passion curses his day — that is, the day of his birth.

On whether the curse was sin the witnesses divide in emphasis. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry calls it “his infirmity”: the extremity of his trouble may excuse it in part, but it cannot be justified, for to curse the day of one's birth because it was the inlet to woe is to quarrel with the God of nature and to despise the dignity of one's being. Yet Henry fixes on the crucial limit — “Job cursed his day, but he did not curse his God”; weary of his life he would gladly have parted with it, but not weary of his religion, which he resolutely cleaves to. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the fault harder: the curse was sinful both because it was vain, being aimed at a thing incapable of blessing or cursing, and because it cast a blame upon God for bringing that day and giving him life on it; still Job does not proceed to curse God, but “makes the devil a liar.” The reformed John Gill reads the opening idiom soberly — “opened his mouth” means simply that Job broke a long silence, having held his peace through the seven days while his friends chose not to speak to him.

A genuine literary question divides the schools. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the striking likeness between this chapter and Jeremiah 20:14-18, and argues that Job is the original — the chapter is indispensable to the development of the poem, whereas in Jeremiah the words fall casually as the record of a passing mood, the prophet quoting Job as he might quote a psalm. Clarke resists any borrowing at all: the resemblance is “no proof that the one borrowed from the other,” but shows only the common Asiatic manner of thinking and feeling on such occasions. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great, facing the harsh literal words, counsels that where the surface of Scripture seems to contradict itself the reader is thereby directed to a truth beneath to be understood — so that Job's imprecation, taken by the letter, drives us to seek the deeper sense, as one traces a stranger's heart only by long and familiar converse.
2:
The formula “Job answered and said” puzzles the witnesses, since no one had addressed him, and they turn the difficulty into a window on the shape of the whole speech. The reformed John Gill observes that the verb rendered “answered” is used even where nothing precedes to which the answer replies; Job “answered to his own calamity, and to their silence,” responding not to speech but to the seven wordless days that had pressed upon him. Gill adds that from this point the book is written in a poetical style, in Hebrew metre as many think — a measure now grown obscure even to the Jews; some have supposed the discourses were not originally delivered in verse but were cast into that form by the writer of the book, and in one Targum the line runs, “And Job sang and said.”

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the accents and to the architecture of the lament. The word for “answered,” they note, signifies to begin to speak from some previous incitement — like the New Testament's “answered” that opens a discourse without a preceding question — and here it marks the exact point where the poetic accentuation begins. The verse itself consists of only three words, divided by the accent Rebia, and its closing “and said” is pointed in an unusual way just because the ordinary form, which always immediately precedes direct speech, would not suit the end of a line.

They then lay out the movement the speech will follow: vv.3-10, the cursing of the day of his birth and the night of his conception; vv.11-19, the eager longing for death; and vv.20-26, the reproachful inquiry why such a life of suffering is prolonged. Some, Keil and Delitzsch report, have named these three movements outright — Schlottmann calling them three strophes, Hahn three parts — the first a delirious cursing of life, the second an eager longing for death, the third a reproachful questioning after the end of such a life of suffering. Yet strophes in any strict sense, they insist, they are not: the progress is one of feeling, delirious cursing passing into a craving for the grave and then into complaint, rather than a measured stanza-form imposed from without. So even this three-word verse, on which the poetic notation first falls, becomes for them the hinge on which the patient sufferer of the two foregoing chapters turns into the lamenting poet of all that follows, the man who through this long conflict will pass, not without sin, yet still triumphantly.
3:
Job's imprecation now takes its form, and the witnesses part at once over what exactly he curses. The reformed John Gill offers two possibilities: either Job wishes the very day of his birth had never been — which is to wish he had never been born, an impossibility Job knows, yet frames to show the greatness of his affliction and his sense of it — or he wishes his birthday, as it returns year after year, to be blotted from the calendar and kept with no feasting or solemnity, struck out of memory and out of the reckoning of days. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch settle firmly on the second: the curse falls on the birthday and the night of conception “as recurring yearly,” not on the actual first day, to which the following imprecations would not be pertinent; Job wishes his birthday to become a dies ater, a black day swallowed up as into nothing.

They dwell on the strange personification of the second line. The clause is elliptical — “the night which said, A man-child is conceived” — and Keil and Delitzsch insist the night itself is the speaker: the night alone was witness of that first beginning of a man's life, and made report of it to the High One to whom it is subordinate. It is not “the night in which they said,” but the night that spoke. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke raises a lexical scruple here: the word commonly rendered “conceived” properly signifies to conceive, yet he judges it should be taken in the sense of being born, since it is unlikely the night of conception could ever be distinctly known or published abroad.

The other voices keep to the plain force of the wish. John Wesley reads it as a prayer that “the remembrance of that day be utterly lost.” The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, tracing the poetry, sets this verse under the first of Job's desires — that earth might forget the day: “Let it perish; let it not be inserted in the calendar,” as the day of a king's nativity is, “but let it be erased and blotted out, and buried in oblivion,” that the world might never know such a man was born into it. The witnesses converge on the extravagance of the passion even as they differ on its reach: whether Job curses the single day now past or its yearly return, whether the night “conceived” or bore him, all agree that a wisdom once famous for its counsel has here, under the reins of grief, wished undone a thing that no wish can undo.
4:
“Let that day be darkness” — and the witnesses insist the darkness Job invokes is no figure but the thing itself. The reformed John Gill is careful on this point: Job does not mean the darkness of calamity, which he would wish on no one and had enough of himself, but literal, gross, dreadful natural darkness. It is the exact reverse of the creating word: where God said “Let there be light,” and called it day, Job wishes his day might be darkness like the night, either never breaking into day at all, or returning ever after remarkably dark and gloomy.

The reach of the second clause — “let not God regard it from above” — the grammatical-historical voices fix with philological care. Charles Ellicott notes that “regard” is literally “require, ask for,” and so “manifest care about” it, comparing the land the LORD's eyes are upon in Deuteronomy 11:12. Keil and Delitzsch render the line “let not Eloah ask after it from above,” so that the day is not merely dark but unsought, uncared for by the God who orders the times. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the same verb the same way: the sense is “let Him not require it,” not count it essential to the completion of the year's days; and if it must be a portion of duration at all, “neither let the light shine upon it” — let it not be distinguished by the sun.

Clarke gathers the whole into the plain image the day deserves: “Let it be blotted out of the calendar.” However distinguished it once was as the birthday of a man renowned for possessions, liberality, and piety, let it now be undistinguished, since he who was so celebrated is become the sport of adversity. John Wesley reads it as the wish that “the sun had never risen upon that day,” and that whenever it returns it may be black and gloomy and uncomfortable. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the verse Job's wish that heaven might frown upon his day: that day is honourable on which God puts honour, but let his birthday be marked, as with a black coal, for an evil day by him that determines the times before appointed — the fountain of light appointing the greater and lesser lights to rule day and night, but this one day left to want the benefit of both. If the light of the day be darkness, Henry adds, how great is that darkness, since then we look for light and find none.
5:
The imprecation deepens — “let darkness and the shadow of death stain it” — and here the witnesses converge on a single disputed verb and pull three renderings from it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke derives the word from the root that gives the goel, the near kinsman whose right it was to redeem an inheritance and to avenge a death: hence he glosses it “pollute or avenge it,” and pictures the day pursued, overtaken, and destroyed — natural darkness, deepened by death's shadow projected over it, seizing on the day as the avenger of blood seizes the offender. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws the same root the other way: “stain” is literally “redeem,” that is, let darkness and the shadow of death “claim it as their rightful inheritance,” the sense that also lies in the reddened garments of Isaiah 63:3 and the polluted table of Malachi 1:7. The reformed John Gill records both possibilities — the darkness of death staining the day, or the alternative “let darkness and the shadow of death redeem it,” challenging and claiming it as their own so that light should have no share in it. Keil and Delitzsch render the line to the same effect, “may darkness and the shadow of death purchase it back.”

On the next clauses Clarke lingers over the imagery. “Let a cloud dwell upon it” he takes to mean that the day should be the very storehouse of the densest vapours, the fixed dwelling-place of the thickest clouds, never dispersed; and the closing words he renders, “let the bitterness of a day fill it with terror.” Ellicott sharpens “blackness of the day” to a preternatural darkness, inopportune and unexpected, like that of an eclipse. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the “shadow of death” as a black shadow like that of the land of the dead, and “stain” as to take away the day's beauty and glory, so that it may be always observed as a frightful and dismal day — the terror falling not on the day only but on men in it.

Clarke completes the picture from the Targum, which likens Job's day to a day of national calamity — such as that on which Jeremiah was distressed for the destruction of the sanctuary, or on which Jonah was cast into the sea, or the day of the darkness that might be felt over the land of Egypt. The witnesses do not finally divide over the sense: whether the darkness “avenges,” “redeems,” or “stains” the day, all read a curse that would hand this one square of time over wholly to night, cloud, and the shadow of death, that no ray might ever reclaim it.
6:
From the day Job turns to the night of his conception — “as for that night, let darkness seize upon it” — and the reformed John Gill marks the shift: having cursed the day he was born, Job now imprecates evils upon the night in which he was conceived, and upon all its yearly returns. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the Targum's paraphrase the surest guide to the whole verse: “Let darkness seize upon that night; let it not be reckoned among the annual festivals; in the number of the months of the calendar let it not be computed.” Some, he adds, take the word for darkness here to mean a dark storm, whence the Vulgate's “dark whirlwind” and Coverdale's “let the dark storm overcome that night.” Clarke draws out the poet's method too: everything is personified — day, night, darkness, the shadow of death, cloud — and through all these verses the imagery is diversified and the expressions varied, while the single idea holds, the total extinction of that portion of time.

A real difference of rendering surfaces in the middle clause. The Authorized reading is “let it not be joined unto the days of the year”; John Wesley keeps it, taking “joined” to mean reckoned as one, or as a part of one, of the year's days. But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects it: rather “let it not rejoice among” the days of the year, as one of the glorious procession of nights. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way — “let it not rejoice among the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months” — so that the night is denied not merely a place in the calendar but any share in the gladness of the ordered times.

Wesley presses the darkness Job asks for to its extreme: a constant and extraordinary darkness, without the least glimmering of light from moon or stars. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the verse under Job's wish that earth might forget his birth, “let it not be joined to the days of the year,” the calendar itself refusing to own it. The witnesses agree on the passion and differ only on the verb: whether the night is merely “not counted” among the year's days, or, as Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch would have it, forbidden to “rejoice” among them — an image that makes the other nights a festal company from which Job's night is cast out.
7:
“Lo, let that night be solitary” — and the witnesses disagree over what the single Hebrew word behind “solitary” most nearly means. The reformed John Gill reads it as barren and desolate: let there be no company for journeys or business, no meetings of friends or kindred, none of the feasts that the night was used for, and especially no marriage-feast; let a silence lie on it as if all creatures were dead. He notes that R. Simeon interprets the word as “barren,” so that the sense is, let no children be born in it, and thus no occasion of joy — let it be as barren as a flint. Keil and Delitzsch render the line to just this effect, “let that night become barren,” childless and fruitless of any gladness.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the word to an Arabic root meaning to cut off, to make bare, whence come the words for a rock and for a heavy burden; and so he draws a different shade of sense: “let that night be grievous, oppressive, as destitute of good as a bare rock is of verdure.” The Targum, he adds, has simply “in that night let there be tribulation.” Clarke marks a small textual point as well — the opening “lo” or “behold” is wanting in one manuscript and unexpressed in the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic — though it changes nothing of the sense. On the second clause all agree with the plain reading, “let no joyful voice come therein,” Clarke taking the word for joyful voice to signify any brisk, cheerful movement, whether of light vibrating or of the voice modulated in a glad song, and reporting the Targum's homely gloss, that not even the crowing of the wild cock should resound in it, but all work be intermitted and every creature fall silent.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse under Job's wish that all joy might forsake his night: “let it be a melancholy night, solitary, and not a merry night of music and dancing; let no joyful voice come therein.” Thus the schools do not so much contradict as color the same darkness differently: to Gill and Keil and Delitzsch the night is barren, emptied of the children and feasts that fill other nights with mirth; to Clarke it is grievous, hard and bare as a stripped rock; and to all it is a night from which every glad sound is banished, that the hour which first gave Job his life might be stripped of all that makes a night worth living through.
8:
This verse is the crux of the whole imprecation, and the witnesses divide sharply over two words — whom Job summons to curse his night, and what those cursers are “ready to raise up.” The Authorized text reads “let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to raise up their mourning,” and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps that sense: let those whose afflictions move them to curse their own birth-day remember Job's and bestow some curses on it; and “mourning” he takes of those who are full of sorrow and always ready to pour out cries and tears, the professional mourners. The reformed John Gill offers a whole range of candidates for “those that curse the day” — adulterers and murderers who rebel against the light; the Ethiopians said to curse the sun at its rising and setting; or hired funeral mourners who in their dirges curse the day a man was born or the day he died.

But the other half of the verse turns on a famous variant. Where the Authorized has “their mourning,” the same Hebrew consonants spell leviathan, and the grammatical-historical and wesleyan-arminian voices prefer it. Keil and Delitzsch render the line “let those who curse the day curse it, who are skilled in stirring up leviathan.” Charles Ellicott reads the cursers as “those who proclaim days unlucky or accursed,” bidden to curse Job's day as pre-eminently so — people “ready to arouse leviathan, or the crocodile, persons as mad and desperate as that,” the most hopeless and reckless of mankind. Adam Clarke translates “let them curse it who detest the day; them who are ready to raise up the leviathan,” and expounds it of those who, weary of life like Job, are desperate enough to provoke the crocodile to tear them; he explicitly rejects the notion of Schultens and others that sorcerers with their execrations are meant, since a man who knew God's sole government as Job did would not appeal to such impostures. Clarke reports Calmet's guess that the Atlantes of Ethiopia are in view, who curse the sun and hunt the crocodile.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both readings in his hand. Under “their mourning” he thinks of those who make it their trade to raise up mourning at funerals with their dirges of lamentation. But he grants that the word is “Leviathan,” and offers two further senses: those who, being about to strike the whale or crocodile, curse it with the bitterest curse they can invent, hoping by incantation to weaken it and master it; or, with Bishop Patrick, those who take Leviathan to mean the devil, so that the cursers are conjurers who raise a devil they cannot lay. So the verse leaves a genuine and unresolved contest: whether Job calls on hired mourners or on desperate men who rouse the crocodile; and whether “leviathan” is the sea-beast of the enchanters' craft or a dark name for the devil himself.
9:
Job carries the curse into the last hours of the night — “let the stars of the twilight thereof be dark” — and the witnesses read the verse as a sustained personification in which the night is denied even the faint comforts that relieve it. The reformed John Gill takes the twilight for either the morning or the evening dusk, rather the latter, and the wish to be that no stars should appear to adorn the heavens, relieve the darkness, and give their guidance to travellers and sailors. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies the “stars of the twilight” with the planets — Venus, Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury — as well as the brighter fixed stars, and finds the personification carried on throughout: the darkness is pictured waiting for the lustre of the evening star, and disappointed; then waiting for the dawn, and equally in vain. Having already prayed that the day's sun should not shine (in v.4), Job now prays that its evening star be obscured and that it never see the dawning — so that his execration takes in everything that might irradiate or enliven the night.

The closing image — “neither let it see the dawning of the day” — the witnesses note is more vivid in the Hebrew. Charles Ellicott gives it literally, “the eyelids of the dawn,” and Keil and Delitzsch render the whole, “let it long for light and there be none, and let it not refresh itself with eyelids of the dawn.” The morning, that is, is imagined opening its eyes upon the world; and Job wishes his night never to catch that first flutter of light.

John Wesley draws the poetic fiction out plainly: the stars, which are the glory and beauty of the night, are to be covered with thick darkness, both in the evening twilight when they begin to shine and on through the night till morning; and the night is made to “look” for light, its darkness aggravated by the disappointment of its own expectation — sense and reasoning ascribed to it, he says, by a poetical figure usual in all writers. The “eyelids of the day” he takes for the morning-star that ushers in the dawn and the first spreading of the light, that this whole natural day of night and morning together might be blotted from the catalogue of days. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds only that Job would have his night so long that it should never “see the eyelids of the morning,” which bring joy with them. The voices do not contend; they agree that the verse personifies the night as a watcher straining for a light that Job forbids it ever to find.
10:
Here Job gives the ground of all his cursing — “because it shut not up the doors of my mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes” — and the witnesses attend both to the strange phrase and to how far the wish reaches. The reformed John Gill notes that “the doors of my womb” is literally “of my belly,” which Aben Ezra referred to the navel, by which the unborn child is nourished; but Gill takes it of the mother's womb, called Job's because he was conceived and borne in it. The complaint, he explains, is laid against the night, either that it did not close the womb and so prevent his conception, or that it did not so shut the womb's doors that he might never have come forth into the world; and he marks a delicate touch — that closing the womb is elsewhere ascribed to God, but Job here lays it on the night, purposely avoiding the name of God, that he might not seem to complain of him or point at him.

The reach of the wish troubles the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, who will not let Job be made to wish his mother's death. It seems very harsh, he says, that a man should desire his mother destroyed in order that his own birth be prevented, and he doubts Job's execration extended so far. He follows the Targum, which understands the umbilical cord: had that been shut up, there must have been a miscarriage, or the child been dead-born, and “so sorrow would have been hidden from his eyes.” This reading, Clarke urges, is nearer the letter of the Hebrew and far more consistent with the feelings of humanity than to wish the mother's womb to have been his grave. John Wesley keeps the plainer sense: the night or day did not keep him from entering this miserable life and experiencing its bitter sorrows.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry stands back to weigh the whole. This, he says, is the ground of Job's quarrel with the day and night of his birth — and it shows the folly and madness of a passionate discontent, which talks so absurdly and extravagantly when the reins are laid on its neck. Is this the Job whose wisdom men once gave ear to and kept silence at his counsel? Surely his wisdom failed him: when he took such pains to wish he had never been, which is a vain wish, for what has been cannot be made not to have been; when he wished a thing so barbarous to his own mother; and when he despised the goodness of God in giving him a being so noble, undervaluing the gift only because it came clogged with a proviso of trouble. So the witnesses hold the verse together — Gill and Wesley reading the closed “doors” of the womb, Clarke softening it to the unshut cord, and Henry lamenting the wisdom that impatience had for the moment overthrown.
11:
The lament now turns from the wish never to have been born to the wish to have died at once, and the reformed John Gill catches the shift: since his conception was not hindered, Job wishes he had died in the womb, or the moment he came from it, “why died I not from the womb?” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads three distinct desires in the verse and the next — dying in the womb, as an abortion never coming to maturity; being still-born, without ever drawing breath; or, if born alive, dying within a short time after; and he thinks Job means each in turn. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add the grammar, noting that the perfect and the interchanging future here carry the force of the oriental subjunctive, the language of a condition that never came to pass — so that Job speaks as one imagining, and mourning, a death that mercifully was not.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the passage at length, and first rebukes its ingratitude. Blessing the barren womb is one thing, he says, recalling the saying our Saviour half-allowed in Luke 23:29, “Blessed are the barren”; but cursing the fruitful womb is another. It is good to make the best of afflictions, but not to make the worst of mercies. Life is often put for all good and death for all evil, yet Job here absurdly complains of life and its supports as a plague and covets the grave as bliss — so that Satan, Henry notes wryly, was quite deceived when he reckoned “all that a man hath will he give for his life,” for never any man valued life at a lower rate than Job now does.

Yet Henry turns the verse into a meditation on the frailty and the mercy of our beginning. It shows, he says, what a weak and helpless creature man is when he comes into the world, and how slender the thread of life is when first drawn: we are ready to die from the womb, able to do nothing for ourselves, and should drop into the grave if the knees did not prevent us and the breasts sustain us. And it shows what tender care divine Providence took of us at our entrance — that we died not from the womb was owing not to our deserving or our strength but to God's power upholding our frail lives and his pity sparing our forfeited ones. “It was of the Lord's mercies that we died not from the womb.” Henry owns that if we had no God to serve here and no better world to hope for, we might well, considering our troubles, wish we had died at birth; but hatred of life contradicts the common sense of mankind, and the man who declaims against it will yet be loath to part with it when it comes to the point — our wisdom being rather, whether living or dying, to be the Lord's, as Romans 14:8 teaches.
12:
“Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck?” — and the witnesses read the verse as Job's complaint against the very first kindnesses shown a newborn. The reformed John Gill asks whose knees are meant, and, against Jarchi's guess of the mother, takes them for the knees of the midwife who received the child into her lap, or of the father, with whom it was an ancient custom — among the Greeks and Romans, and reflected in the name of the goddess Levana — to take the newborn on his knees in token of owning it. Job's grievance is that he did not fall to the ground as he came from the womb and there die, but was caught and cherished by those officious knees, and had all the usual things done to preserve his life.

The word “prevent” the witnesses take in its old sense of coming before, meeting, forestalling. Charles Ellicott glosses the whole with a hard clarity: “Why was I nursed with care instead of being allowed to fall to the ground and be killed?” John Wesley expands it in the same key — why did the midwife or nurse receive and lay him on her knees, and not suffer him to fall upon the bare ground till death had taken him from this miserable world, into which, he says, “their cruel kindness hath betrayed me”; and why did the breasts prevent him from perishing of hunger. Thus, Wesley remarks, Job unthankfully despises these wonderful mercies of God toward poor helpless infants. Adam Clarke reads the two clauses simply as the dandling on the knees and the nourishing at the breast, without which he had been received into no mother's lap nor hung upon any mother's breast.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same details into his meditation on infant frailty. The lamp of life, when first lighted, would go out of itself, he says, if the breasts given us did not supply it with fresh oil; and it was natural affection, put into parents' hearts by the hand of the God of nature, that made the blessings of the breast attend those of the womb. So the witnesses agree in reading the verse as a passionate ingratitude that Job would afterward be ashamed of: the knees that caught him and the breasts that fed him, which every eye but a sufferer's would call mercies, he here arraigns as the cruel means by which he was kept alive for sorrow — charging as unkindness the tenderest providence that watches over the helpless at their entrance into the world.
13:
Job now turns from the death he was spared to the rest he imagines it would have brought — “for now should I have lain still, and been quiet; I should have slept: then had I been at rest.” The reformed John Gill draws out the comparison hidden in the words: had he died at birth he would long since have been laid in the grave, which is to the dead what a bed is to the living, only more restful; for on a bed there is often tossing and disquiet, but the body in the grave is wholly still and silent, free from all the care and anxiety and pain that now beset him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the four verbs as an ascending calm: in that case he had been insensible; quiet, without these overwhelming agitations; he had slept, unconscious of evil; and been at rest, out of the reach of calamity and sorrow.

Keil and Delitzsch render the line to the same sense — “so should I now have lain and had quiet, I should have slept, then it would have been well with me” — the whole strophe unfolding what death would have secured. The force falls on that word “now”: over against the tossing, sleepless, restless man he actually is, Job sets the still figure he might have been, so that the verse measures his present torment by the peace he pictures losing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the poignancy and the poverty of the hope together. “Then should I have lain still and been quiet, which now I cannot do,” for now he is still tossing and unquiet; “then I should have slept,” whereas now sleep departs from his eyes; “then had I been at rest,” whereas now he is restless. Yet Henry notes what Job's hope does not reach: all the poor sufferer dreams of is rest and quietness in the grave, out of the fear of evil tidings and the feeling of sore boils, whereas the gospel gives the believer a better account of the gain of death — to be present with the Lord and see his glory. And Henry adds a searching aside: had Job but kept the even, easy temper of the two foregoing chapters, entirely resigned to God's will, he might have been quiet even now, his soul dwelling at ease though his body lay in pain, as Psalms 25:13 promises. The rest he covets in the grave was, in part, to be had already in submission.
14:
Job imagines the company his early death would have given him — “with kings and counsellors of the earth” — and the witnesses read the verse as a meditation on the levelling power of the grave. The reformed John Gill allows that Job, a man of great distinction, might have descended from such, and been buried in his fathers' sepulchres in pomp; but the deeper point is that death spares none, that neither the power of kings with their long reach nor the wisdom of counsellors with their long heads can secure them, so that after death they are on a level with all others — even, he adds, with children who died at birth and made no figure in the world.

The obscure phrase “which built desolate places for themselves” divides the witnesses. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it of the great sepulchral monuments — the mausoleums, funeral pyramids, and tombs by which kings sought to keep their names from perishing while their bodies turned to corruption — and he expressly rejects the reading that would make these patriotic princes who repaired the ruins others had made; the simple idea, he says, is that Job would have been as much at rest as these mighty agitators of the world, who now have nothing to shield even their names but the monuments that hold their mouldering bones. Charles Ellicott reads it much the same — gorgeous tombs and splendid sepulchres, desolate because tenanted only by the dead, or else places once built that are now themselves ruined; in the former sense, he thinks, the Pyramids may be hinted at. Keil and Delitzsch render it flatly, kings “who built ruins for themselves.” But John Wesley takes the other road: these are men who, to show their wealth and power or leave a glorious name, rebuilt ruined cities or raised new cities and palaces in places that before were mere solitude and waste.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry embraces both the tombs and the buried treasure, and turns all to the one lesson. Some, he says, understand the “desolate places” of the sepulchres the great prepared for themselves in their lifetime, as Shebna hewed himself a tomb in Isaiah 22:16, and the gold and silver of the treasures men once laid in the graves of the mighty; but such arts to preserve their dignity beyond death will not serve, for “death is, and will be, an irresistible leveller” — death mingles sceptres with spades. Rich and poor meet together in the grave, and there, Henry says, a hidden untimely birth lies as soft and safe as kings and counsellors and princes that had gold; “and therefore,” he has Job cry, “would I had lain there in the dust, rather than lie here in the ashes.”
15:
The roll of the mighty dead continues — “or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver” — and the witnesses read it as one more proof that wealth is no fence against the grave. The reformed John Gill observes that these seem to be princes whose greatness lay not in ruling a particular land but in their abundance of riches, having a large store of gold while they lived and their houses filled with silver; yet now, being dead, they possess it no longer and are on a level with those who had none, for their gold could neither preserve them from death while they had it, nor remain theirs, nor do them any good once they had died. Death makes the wealthiest prince equal with the poorest child, and the untimely birth that Job envies lies as easy as the richest of them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke describes them as the chief and mighty men, lords of the soil or fortunate adventurers in merchandise, who got gold in abundance and filled their houses with silver, and then “left all behind, and had nothing reserved for themselves but the empty places which they had made for their last dwelling.” There their dust now sleeps, devoid of care and painful journeys and anxious expectation. Clarke draws in an Eastern proverb of Saady's on the covetous, whom nothing can satisfy but the dust that at last fills his mouth in the grave — the only portion of all his hoard that the rich man carries down with him.

Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet plainly, “princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver,” setting it beside the kings and counsellors of the preceding verse as another rank of the great whom death has equalized. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the thought into his refrain on the levelling grave: even princes who had gold in abundance could not with it bribe Death to overlook them when he came with commission, and though they filled their houses with silver they were forced to leave it all behind, no more to return to it. So the witnesses agree in reading the verse not as envy of the great but as consolation drawn from the grave's impartiality — that the untimely birth Job wishes he had been would lie as securely as the richest prince, for gold buys no exemption from the common dust, and the silver-filled house is exchanged, at last, for a narrow and empty room.
16:
Job names the lowest and least of the dead as company he would gladly have kept — “or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light.” The reformed John Gill renders it with Broughton “hid, as one born out of time,” and notes it is the very word the apostle uses of himself in 1 Corinthians 15:8; the term carries the sense of falling, and so denotes an abortive birth, fruit that falls from the tree before it is ripe. Such a birth is “hidden,” whether in the womb, as the Targum has it, or simply from human sight, having come to no proper shape; and Job's thought is that, even if he could not have lain among kings and princes, he might at least have been as this — and that would have served him as well.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke distinguishes the two figures of the verse. The “hidden untimely birth” he takes for an early miscarriage, scarcely perceptible even by the mother, in which case the child never had so much as the distinguishable form of a human being, whether male or female — “he had not been.” The “infants which never saw light” he reads as little ones farther advanced toward maturity, yet miscarried long before the time of birth. Charles Ellicott adds only that this is another of the conditions Job names which would have relieved him from the experience of suffering — one more form of the not-being he covets. John Wesley glosses “hidden” as undiscerned and unregarded, born before the due time and so never come into the land of the living.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the untimely birth at the climax of the grave's great equality. There, he says, a hidden untimely birth — a child that either never saw the light, or but just opened its eyes on the world and, not liking it, closed them again and hastened out of it — lies as soft and easy, as high and safe, as kings and counsellors and princes that had gold. The witnesses do not divide on the pathos of it: Job, in the depth of his misery, reaches past all rank and wealth to envy the very abortion that never drew breath, because it never knew sorrow. That the least and most obscure of all human beginnings should seem to him a happier lot than his own is the measure of how heavy his life has grown.
17:
“There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest” — and the witnesses linger over the double peace of the grave, rest for the troublers and the troubled alike. The reformed John Gill reads the wicked as those who, like the troubled sea that cannot rest, were always devising or doing mischief while they lived, but in the grave can do neither, “for there is no work nor device there”; persecutors and false teachers and cruel oppressors, when they die, cease from giving trouble, and a good man at death is troubled no more by wicked men, nor even by his own wicked heart, nor by Satan. Charles Ellicott adds the grammarian's small note that “there” means the grave, the place indicated by the whole passage though not distinctly named.

The wesleyan-arminian voices set the two ranks in sharp opposition. Adam Clarke: in the grave the oppressors of men cease from irritating, harassing, and distressing their fellow-creatures, and there the weary — those worn out by the cruelties and tyrannies of the great — are at rest; the toils of the mighty and the labours of the slave are alike ended. John Wesley reads it the same way: the great oppressors and troublers of the world cease from their vexations, rapines, and murders, and those who were molested and tired out by their tyrannies now quietly sleep beside them. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet “there the wicked cease from troubling, and the weary are at rest,” noting that the word for the wicked's “troubling” carries the root-idea of restless commotion, the tossing of the troubled sea, while the word for the rest of the weary denotes a perfect freedom from care.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the comfort out fully. Those that now are troubled will there be out of the reach of trouble: when persecutors die they can no longer persecute, and their hatred and envy perish with them — Herod vexed the church, but when he became a prey for worms he ceased from troubling. And those that are now toiled will there see the period of their toils: heaven is more than a rest to the souls of the saints, but the grave is a rest to their bodies; their weary pilgrimage over, they rest from all their labours, as Revelation 14:13 declares, and sleep in Jesus. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in Job's words a true, if partial, description of the grave's repose — partial, Henry hints, because Job dreams only of the body's quiet, where grace can promise the soul's rest in God as well.
18:
The catalogue of the grave's peace comes to the captive and the slave — “there the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor.” The reformed John Gill reads it of those who in life lay in prison for debt, or were condemned to the galleys, or suffered bonds for religion's sake: at death their chains are knocked off, and they are as much at liberty and ease as the dead who were never prisoners — resting not only beside their fellow-prisoners but on a level with those who never saw a prison, and even with the very men who cast them into one. Keil and Delitzsch render the line “the captives dwell together in tranquillity; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster,” the emphasis falling on that untroubled repose.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the “oppressor,” whom he takes for the hard, unrelenting taskmaster whose voice was more terrible than death itself; in the grave the slaves who felt all the troubles and scarcely tasted the pleasures of life are quiet together, free from his exactions, his mouth silenced in the dust. He hears in it a possible echo of the Egyptian bondage, when the children of Israel cried by reason of their taskmasters. Charles Ellicott confirms the hint philologically: the word rendered “oppressor” is the same rendered “taskmaster” in the story of the oppression, as when the taskmasters drove Israel in Exodus 5:6, so that some have thought an allusion to that history lies here.

John Wesley reads the oppressor as the one who urges and forces men to work by cruel threats and stripes, and adds an important limit to the whole passage: Job does not here meddle with the eternal state of men after death, of which he speaks later, but only with their freedom from worldly troubles, which is the sole matter of his present discourse. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry agrees that death is the prisoner's discharge, the relief of the oppressed, and the servant's manumission: there the prisoners, though they walk not at large, yet rest together and are not put to grind in the prison-house, no more insulted or terrified by their cruel taskmasters, for they hear not the voice of the oppressor; those doomed here to a perpetual servitude, who could call nothing their own, not even their own bodies, are there no longer under command or control. The witnesses converge on a grave that is, for the captive, a kind of jubilee — the one place where the driver's shout can no longer reach the driven.
19:
The list closes on the great equation of the tomb — “the small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master.” The reformed John Gill takes “small and great” of every difference among men, whether of age and stature or of estate and dignity: children and men, the lowly and the exalted, the poor and the rich, all come to the grave without distinction and lie there without difference, “little and great” all one. The servant, bound in life, is there discharged from his lord.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the verse a set-piece on human equality. All sorts and conditions of men are blended in the grave and reduced to one common dust, and between the bond and the free there is no difference; the grave is the appointed rendezvous where all travellers meet. Men begin and end life alike, and all the intermediate state is disparity; a contemplation that should humble the great and the small together. He crowns it with the classics — Horace's line that pale Death knocks with equal foot at the poor man's hut and the king's tower, and a long passage from Seneca's letter to Marcia on how death, in spite of the master, manumits the slave, loosens the prisoner's chains, and reduces to one level all whom fortune had unequally divided. John Wesley reads it as persons of all qualities and conditions being in the same place and state, every earthly distinction forever abolished, and draws the moral: a good reason why those who have power should use it moderately, and those in subjection should bear it patiently.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his theme of the grave as leveller: the small and great are there, there the same, there all one, all alike free among the dead; the tedious pomp and state that attend the great are at an end, and all the inconveniences of a poor and low condition are over, for death and the grave know no difference. The witnesses do not contend; they read in Job's closing image a strange consolation — that the very tomb he longs for would set him among kings and beside slaves without regard to either, so that the servant is free from his master and the master no greater than his servant, and the sorrows that rank had multiplied are, in that one place, wholly undone. It is a double-edged comfort, for the same levelling that eases the slave humbles the prince; but to Job, stripped and afflicted, the equality of the grave is precisely its attraction, since there at last the distinctions that made his fall so public would count for nothing at all.
20:
Job's lament turns from longing for the grave to the reproachful question that governs the rest of the chapter — “wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul?” The reformed John Gill reads “light” as life, the light of the living, which is sweet to a man in health but not to one in Job's pain of body and anguish of mind, who would rather be in the dark and silent grave. He notes a reverent delicacy in the Hebrew: the words may be rendered “wherefore does he give light?” — God being meant, though not named, out of reverence, that Job might not seem to quarrel with him; for the principle of life, and its protraction, and all that supports it, are God's gift.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same suppressed reference: “why doth he give light?” Job means God, yet does not name him, tacitly reflecting on Providence as unkind in continuing life when life's comforts are gone. Life is called light, Henry says, because it is pleasant and serviceable for walking and working; it is candle-light, the longer it burns the shorter it grows and the nearer to the socket, and it is given, for if it were not daily renewed to us by fresh gift it would go out. But to those in misery, he adds, it becomes “a gift and no gift,” a gift they had better be without, since the light only serves them to see their own misery by. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the question briefly and sharply: why is life granted to him who is incapable of enjoying it or of performing its functions? John Wesley glosses the terms — light is the light of life, given because daily renewed to us, and “bitter” names those to whom life itself has become bitter and burdensome.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the deliberate pairing of light and life, comparing the fountain of life and light in Psalms 36:9 and the life that was the light of men in John 1:4. Behind the particular complaint the latin-fathers Gregory the Great sets the whole hidden problem it raises — why in this life it is sometimes ill with the good and well with the wicked. God's appointments are deeply hidden, he says: the good, if they have done any wrong, may receive their punishment here that they may be the more completely freed hereafter, while the wicked meet with the good things of this life that they may be dragged to unmitigated torments after it. So Job's question — why light to the wretched — opens upon the darkest of the mysteries of providence, which the book will spend all its length exploring.
21:
Job describes the sufferers who would welcome the death that will not come — “which long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures.” The reformed John Gill dwells on the straining of the desire: they earnestly wish and wistfully look for death, gaping for it as a hungry man for his food or a fisherman for his catch, yet it comes not to their wish, because its fixed time is not yet. Death, he cautions, is not desirable in itself, being the dissolution of nature and the wages of sin; it may be lawfully desired by good men — that they may be free from sin and be with the Lord — but such desire should be expressed with submission to God's will and should wait his appointed time, not be craved merely to be rid of present afflictions.

The image of the second line the witnesses take literally. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole, “who wait for death, and he comes not, who dig after him more than for treasure” — the longing pictured as a digging, more eager than the search for buried gold. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it plainly: they long for death as the end of all their miseries, and long more for a separation from life than lovers of gold do for a rich mine. John Wesley makes the same comparison — they “desire it with as much earnestness as men dig for treasure” — but he marks a restraint in Job that guards the whole from despair: for all his miseries, Job durst do nothing to hasten or procure his own death, but was content to wait all the days of his appointed time till his change should come, as he will say in Job 14:14.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the diggers as those who would give anything for a fair dismission from the world; and he notes with approval what the verse quietly assumes — that the thought of a man's being his own executioner was not so much as entertained here, else those who longed for death need not have dug so hard for it, but might soon have come at it. So the witnesses hold two things together: the reality of a grief so deep that death seems a treasure to be mined for, and the sober fence around it — that longing for release, however lawful when tempered by submission, must leave the time and manner in the hand of God, who alone appoints when the change shall come.
22:
The longing rises to its height — “which rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave.” The reformed John Gill, following Broughton, renders it “which joy till they do skip again,” so elated at the prospect of the grave that they leap and dance for joy — the strongest possible figure for a gladness that most men reserve for the height of prosperity, here fixed instead upon a tomb. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet with the same intensity, “who rejoice with exceeding joy, who are enraptured, when they can find the grave.”

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes a textual point in the verse. The received reading is “they rejoice with joy,” and exult when they find the grave; but he records a variant in one of Kennicott's manuscripts which, by a single letter, turns “with joy” into “at the tomb,” so that the line would run, “who rejoice at the Tomb, and exult when they find the grave” — the object of the gladness made doubly plain. Either way the sense is one: a joy that fastens on the very place all other men dread, so that the grave, which is the last terror of the living, becomes to these sufferers the one thing they hunt for and hail with rapture when at length it is found.

John Wesley lifts his eye from the description to its moral, warning against the mood Job here voices. To be thus impatient of life for the sake of the troubles we meet with, he says, is not only unnatural in itself but ungrateful to the Giver of life, and shows a sinful indulgence of our own passion; let it rather be our great and constant care to get ready for another world, and then leave it to God to order the circumstances of our removal thither as he thinks fit. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the last of Job's three postures toward death — those who long for it, those who dig for it, and here those who bid it welcome and are glad when they can find the grave and see themselves stepping into it. If the miseries of this life can, contrary to nature, make death itself desirable, Henry reflects, how much more should the hopes of a better life set us above the fear of it. The witnesses agree that Job's gladness at the grave is real and deep, and that its very extravagance is the measure of a suffering that has turned the common order of desire upside down.
23:
Job draws the general complaint back to his own case — “why is light given to a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in?” The reformed John Gill offers two ways to take “whose way is hid.” It may mean that Job's way is hidden from God, neglected and overlooked, so that the injuries done him go unregarded, as the church complains elsewhere; or, more likely, that the way of the Lord is hidden from Job — the reasons of the present afflictive providence which he cannot understand, not being conscious of any notorious sin that should bring such troubles down. Either way, the man walks in a darkness of mind to match the darkness of his estate.

The clause “whom God hath hedged in” the witnesses read as the sign of a shut and hopeless path. Adam Clarke glosses it of one who knows not what is before him in either world but is full of fears, hedged about so that no way of escape is left and he cannot see a step ahead; he finds an exact parallel in the mourner of Lamentations who cries that God “hath hedged me about that I cannot get out” and “inclosed my ways with hewn stone” in Lamentations 3:7. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches a sharp irony in the word: the very same expression was used in the opposite sense in Job 1:10, where Satan complained that God had made a hedge about Job to protect him and all he had. The hedge that was once his shelter has become his prison.

John Wesley reads it in the same key — the way hid from Job, who knows not which way to turn to comfort himself in his miseries, and God having put him as it were in a prison, so that he can see no way or possibility of escape. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds that Job saw no way open of deliverance nor knew what course to take; his way was hedged up with thorns that he could not find his path, and his great grief was that he knew not wherefore God contended with him. The witnesses converge on the pathos of the enclosed sufferer — a man denied both the light of comfort and the light of understanding, and cruelly given the light of life he no longer wants, precisely because the hedge that once guarded him now hems him in.
24:
Job turns from the general question to the raw evidence of his own days — “for my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters.” The reformed John Gill takes the first clause temporally: before he sits down to eat, before he has so much as tasted his food, there is nothing but sighing and sobbing, so that he has no appetite, and even while he eats his tears mingle with the meal, the bread and water of affliction being his continual portion. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers two accounts of it — either, with Origen, that Job's ulcerated body could not lift the food to his mouth or chew it, or, more naturally, that his sighing took away all appetite and served him in the place of meat, as the psalmist's tears were his meat day and night in Psalms 42:3 — and he pictures the “roarings” as the noise of a murmuring stream or the dashing of an overswollen torrent.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the first line otherwise, turning on the small preposition. It is not “before I eat” but “instead of my food”: “for instead of my food my sighing cometh, and my roarings pour themselves forth as water.” The particle, they argue, passes here from the local sense to the substitutionary, as the Latin pro, the same usage that appears in Job 4:19; sighing has become the very nourishment that bread should be. So a genuine difference of rendering runs beneath the verse — Gill, Clarke, and Wesley reading that the sighing comes before the meal, Keil and Delitzsch that it comes in place of it — though both amount to a man whose grief has swallowed up his hunger.

John Wesley expounds “before the face of my bread” as meaning that all the time he is eating he falls into sighing and weeping, because he is forced to eat and support this wretched life, and because of his uninterrupted pains of body and mind that grant him no quiet moment; and the “roarings” he takes for loud outcries, more befitting a lion than a man, poured out with great abundance and irresistible violence, as waters break their banks and overflow the ground. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same picture as proof that Job had no comfort of his life: his sorrows returned as duly as his meals, so that affliction was his daily bread, and he did not only sigh but roar, his roarings poured out like waters in a full and constant stream. The witnesses agree on the misery and divide only on the grammar — whether the sighing comes before the food or instead of it.
25:
Job traces his ruin back to the very fears he had carried in his prosperity — “for the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me.” The witnesses divide over whether, and how, so faithful a man really harboured such fears. The reformed John Gill inclines to doubt it: the words might refer to Job's fears for his children, lest they should sin and bring down judgment, or to a general dread of the changes of the world; but Gill thinks it hardly reasonable that a man of Job's faith and trust should indulge such fears to that degree, or ever surmise that calamities so shocking should befall him, and so he will not read the verse of Job's former life in prosperity at all.

The other witnesses take it the plainer way, that Job in his ease did foresee and dread adversity. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders the Hebrew “I feared a fear,” and expounds: while in prosperity he thought adversity might come, and dreaded it; he feared the loss of his family and his property, and both have now occurred. Yet Clarke hears no self-reproach in it — “I was not lifted up,” Job means; he knew what he possessed he held from divine Providence, who might give and take away, and so he is not stripped as a punishment for presumption. John Wesley reads the fear as habitual and godly: even in prosperity Job was full of fears, considering the variety of God's providences, the changeableness of this vain world, God's justice, and the sinfulness of all mankind; and those fears, he says, were not in vain, but are justified by his present calamities.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the verse beside the man who is “happy that feareth alway” in Proverbs 28:14: Job had always kept in remembrance the uncertainty and instability of earthly things, and yet had been overtaken by a calamity that mocked his carefulness and exceeded his apprehensions. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet with a shudder of feeling — “for I fear something terrible, and it cometh upon me, and that before which I shudder cometh to me.” The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the point of it in Job's blameless vigilance: he had not been negligent of his affairs, but kept up such a fear of trouble as was needed to keep his guard — afraid for his children when they were feasting, lest they should offend God, as Job 1:5 records — and yet all his precaution could not keep the trouble off. So the witnesses circle a real difference: whether Job's fear was the anxious foreboding of one who saw the world's frailty clearly, as Clarke, Wesley, and Ellicott hold, or something Gill can scarcely credit of so settled a faith.
26:
The chapter ends on a line of broken rest — “I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came.” The witnesses divide over whether Job here looks back on his prosperity or denies he ever had any peace at all. The reformed John Gill holds firmly that the words cannot refer to the time of his prosperity, for then he certainly was in safety, God having set a hedge about him so that neither his enemies nor Satan himself could reach him to do him hurt; the unrest Job describes must belong to his present estate.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the opposite way, and suggests the verse be taken as a question: “Was I not in safety? had I not rest? was I not in comfort? yet trouble came” — for it is well known that before this assault Job was in great prosperity and peace, and the sense is of evils treading on each other's heels, one wave following another as in the psalmist's “deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts” in Psalms 42:7; he notes that Mr. Good renders it “I had no peace, yea, I had no rest,” referring the whole to the swift succession of Job's heavy trials. John Wesley reads the line as Job's plea of a good conscience in his former ease: “I did not misbehave myself in prosperity, abusing it by presumption and security, but I lived circumspectly, walking humbly with God, and working out my salvation with fear and trembling” — and so, in this sense too, his way was hidden, for he knew not why God contended with him.

Keil and Delitzsch render the close with the same restlessness, “I dwelt not in security, nor rested, nor refreshed myself: then trouble cometh,” the sudden present tense letting the calamity break in upon the verse as it broke in upon the man. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reconciles the readings: even in his prosperous state Job was never careless or secure, but kept so much fear of trouble as maintained his guard, and had not trusted in his wealth nor flattered himself that his mirth would last — yet trouble came, to convince him of the world's vanity. So the great lament closes where it must, on the plain fact that no prudence and no piety had fenced the trouble out; and the witnesses, whether they read a lost peace or a peace Job denies he ever fully had, agree that the last word of the chapter is the arrival of the very trouble against which no watchfulness could avail — the door through which the long debate of his friends is about to open.
